source.title: Deep Learning in Brain MRI: Effect of Data Leakage Due to Slice-level Split Using 2D Convolutional Neural Networks
source.authors: Ekin Yağış; S. Atnafu; A. G. S. de Herrera; Chiara Marzi; M. Giannelli; C. Tessa; L. Citi; S. Diciotti

record.file_problem: The full text is present; no apparent cutoff or corruption affecting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests random-label performance under two data-splitting methods and shows that slice-level leakage produces high test accuracy, while subject-level results are near chance and training accuracy varies by model.
record.gate_note: Table 4 reports training and test accuracy for the OASIS-random dataset under subject-level and slice-level splits. Other datasets and results are outside these claim versions. The study does not report training time, unstructured-input fits, noise fractions, regularization comparisons, or learning order.
record.test_reason: Table 4 measures fitting randomized subject labels in a new MRI setting. It bears on V1, although labels are shared across each subject's slices, training lasts 50 epochs, and hyperparameters are selected by validation performance rather than held fixed across label conditions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: slice-level splitting severely inflates apparent test performance, including approximately 95% accuracy with randomized subject labels, whereas subject-level splitting yields approximately 50%. The authors recommend subject-level cross-validation for 2D analysis of 3D MRI data.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pre-trained 2D MRI CNNs and nested cross-validation to compare subject-level and slice-level splits; it does not reproduce the original random-labeling experiments on their original settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome changes markedly with the data split: subject-level versus slice-level splitting.

fits_no_version.finding: Slice-level splitting yields 95.93%, 94.81% and 93.74% test accuracy despite randomized subject labels because training and test sets share subjects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Correlated slices from the same subject can inflate held-out slice accuracy through subject leakage, even when subject labels are random.

record.problems: The authors note substantial overfitting under subject-level splits; training accuracy is much higher than test accuracy. The random-label experiment is on an OASIS-derived MRI dataset and its results depend strongly on the split strategy. No uncertainty estimates are reported for Table 4 values.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant Table 4 rows left out; the rows cover all three models, both split methods, and training and test accuracy for OASIS-random.

untested.parts: Independent random labels for individual slices; fitting after training to convergence; unchanged selected hyperparameters between true and random labels; independent-subject test performance for the models trained with slice-level splits.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence as corruption increases. Reported computational times are grouped by architecture and dataset size.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test performance across intermediate label-corruption fractions.
Effects of adding or removing weight decay, dropout, or augmentation.
Learning order for real patterns versus noisy labels; no training trajectories are reported.

record.verdict_notes: All Table 4 values are correctly extracted. The supplied text is the published Scientific Reports article, DOI 10.1038/s41598-021-01681-w, although the record identifier names a preprint. Table 4 specifies fivefold nested CV, while the methods prose specifies tenfold; the discrepancy is unresolved.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests random labels with three MRI CNN models and two split strategies. It does not test the original sources' image datasets or establish results for standard deep networks generally.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Training accuracy is not near 100% for any tested model (R1, R3, R5), while test accuracy is around the stated 50% chance expectation (R2, R4, R6). This challenges fitting random labels in this setting.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: All three models reach near-perfect training accuracy, but test accuracy is far above chance under the leakage-prone split (R7–R12).
